<!-- nogotheorem-1: body_md -->
\label{thm:orbit-trilemma}
For $N\ge k$, the family \eqref{eq:kbody} satisfies
\begin{equation}
 \Xi_N^{(k)}=\binom{N-1}{k-1}|J_N|\left\lVert h\right\rVert.
 \label{eq:incident-exact}
\end{equation}
Consequently it cannot simultaneously possess:
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
\item exact $S_N$ covariance with no prescribed support hypergraph;
\item a volume-independent lower bound $|J_N|\ge J_0>0$;
\item a volume-uniform incident-norm bound;
\item finite interaction range in metrics $d_N$ whose diameters diverge.
\end{enumerate}
Kac scaling can enforce (iii) only by taking
$J_N=O(N^{1-k})$; for nonzero couplings it does not repair (iv).
The incident quantity in \eqref{eq:incident} is a sum of term norms,
not an asserted lower bound on the operator norm of the full Hamiltonian.
Retaining only $O(1)$ terms
incident on each site introduces either a background support hypergraph or a
dynamical support observable.
<!-- end nogotheorem-1 -->
<!-- proof-1: body_md -->
The orbit of one $k$-subset under $S_N$ is the complete family
$\binom{[N]}k$.  Exactly $\binom{N-1}{k-1}$ members of that orbit contain a
fixed site, proving \eqref{eq:incident-exact}.  If $|J_N|\ge J_0$, the right
side grows as $N^{k-1}$.

Suppose instead that the interaction terms have metric range at most a
fixed $R$ and $J_N\ne0$.  By the minimal-support assumption,
each nonzero embedded term has support exactly $X$.  Given distinct
$i,j$ and $N\ge k$, some $k$-subset $X$ contains both.  Complete orbit support then implies $d_N(i,j)\le R$.  Hence
$\operatorname{diam}([N],d_N)\le R$, contradicting a diverging diameter.  Scaling $J_N$
does not alter support.  Finally, deleting almost all orbit terms requires
additional information specifying which subsets survive.  If fixed, it is
background structure; if represented by quantum degrees of freedom, locality
is sector dependent.
<!-- end proof-1 -->
<!-- nogotheorem-2: body_md -->
\label{thm:orbit-degeneracy}
Let
\begin{equation}
 H_{\mathrm{diag}}=\sum_{G\in\mathfrak G_N}E(G)\lvert G\rangle\!\langle G\rvert
 \label{eq:diag-graph-H}
\end{equation}
be diagonal in the graph basis and satisfy
\(U_\pi H_{\mathrm{diag}}U_\pi^\dagger=H_{\mathrm{diag}}\) for every
\(\pi\in S_N\).  If \(G\) is a ground graph, then every graph in its orbit is
a ground graph and
\begin{equation}
 \dim\operatorname{ker}(H_{\mathrm{diag}}-E_0\mathbf 1)
 \ge |S_N\!\cdot G|
 =\frac{N!}{|\operatorname{Aut}(G)|}.
 \label{eq:orbit-degeneracy}
\end{equation}
A unique graph-basis ground state is possible only when \(G\) is fixed by all
of \(S_N\); among simple graphs this leaves only the empty and complete graphs.
Consequently, a nonempty noncomplete sparse graph cannot be selected as a
unique classical vacuum by an exactly permutation-invariant diagonal energy.
<!-- end nogotheorem-2 -->
<!-- proof-2: body_md -->
Permutation covariance and diagonality give \(E(\pi G)=E(G)\).  Hence the
entire orbit of a minimizing graph lies in the ground space.  Orbit--stabilizer
gives Eq.~\eqref{eq:orbit-degeneracy}.  If the orbit has one element, the edge
set is invariant under the transitive action of \(S_N\) on unordered pairs.
It is therefore either empty or the full pair set.
<!-- end proof-2 -->
<!-- corollary-1: body_md -->
\label{cor:robust-orbit-gap}
Let \(H_{\mathrm{diag}}\) be diagonal in the graph basis and define its
permutation-covariance defect
\begin{equation}
 \delta_{\mathrm{sym}}
 :=\max_{\pi\in S_N}
 \left\|U_\pi H_{\mathrm{diag}}U_\pi^\dagger-H_{\mathrm{diag}}\right\|.
 \label{eq:symmetry-defect}
\end{equation}
Suppose \(\lvert G\rangle\) is a unique graph-basis ground state and let
\begin{equation}
 \gamma_G:=\min_{G'\ne G}\bigl[E(G')-E(G)\bigr]>0
 \label{eq:graph-gap}
\end{equation}
be its classical basis gap.  Then either \(G\) is empty or complete, or
\begin{equation}
 \gamma_G\le\delta_{\mathrm{sym}}.
 \label{eq:robust-orbit-gap}
\end{equation}
Thus a nontrivial labeled graph vacuum can be unique only at the price of a
symmetry defect at least as large as its protecting gap.
<!-- end corollary-1 -->
<!-- proof-3: body_md -->
For every permutation \(\pi\),
\begin{align}
 |E(\pi G)-E(G)|
 &=\left|\langle G\rvert
 \bigl(U_\pi^\dagger H_{\mathrm{diag}}U_\pi-H_{\mathrm{diag}}\bigr)
 \lvert G\rangle\right|\\
 &\le\delta_{\mathrm{sym}}.
\end{align}
If the orbit of \(G\) is nontrivial, choose \(\pi G\ne G\).  Uniqueness gives
\(E(\pi G)-E(G)\ge\gamma_G\), proving
Eq.~\eqref{eq:robust-orbit-gap}.  A singleton orbit is empty or complete by
\Cref{thm:orbit-degeneracy}.
<!-- end proof-3 -->
<!-- remark-1: body_md -->
The theorem concerns a unique \emph{graph-basis} vacuum of a diagonal
Hamiltonian.  An off-diagonal, permutation-invariant operator may select a
unique orbit superposition.  Such a state is not one labeled classical graph;
it requires coherent orbit mixing and leaves classical geometry to a further
measurement, decoherence, or symmetry-breaking analysis.
<!-- end remark-1 -->
<!-- corollary-2: body_md -->
\label{cor:staged}
Under the hypotheses of \Cref{thm:orbit-trilemma,thm:orbit-degeneracy}, a
permutation-covariant model with no hidden geometry must distinguish at least
three logically separate ingredients before claiming a physical finite-range
propagation law: a prelocal microscopic operator, selection of a sparse relational
sector, and a sectorwise quasillocality estimate such as a Lieb--Robinson bound
\cite{LiebRobinson1972}.
<!-- end corollary-2 -->
<!-- remark-2: body_md -->
The theorem concerns complete interaction orbits.  It does not assert that
permutation symmetry forbids locality after spontaneous or relational sector
selection.  It forbids treating the selected metric support as already present
at the same logical level as the exact microscopic symmetry.
<!-- end remark-2 -->
<!-- nogotheorem-3: body_md -->
\label{thm:connectivity}
Fix $r<\infty$.  No functional of $(|V(G)|,\mathsf P_r(G))$ can vanish on all
connected finite graphs and be strictly positive on all disconnected finite
graphs.  In particular, neither a fixed-radius additive energy nor an arbitrary
postprocessing of all radius-$r$ neighborhood counts can detect connectedness
exactly.
<!-- end nogotheorem-3 -->
<!-- proof-4: body_md -->
Choose $n\ge\max\{3,2r+2\}$.  The connected cycle $C_{2n}$ and the disconnected graph
$C_n\sqcup C_n$ have the same number $2n$ of vertices.  Every rooted
radius-$r$ ball in either graph is the path on $2r+1$ vertices rooted at its
center.  Their profiles \eqref{eq:profile} are therefore identical, although
one graph is connected and the other is not.
<!-- end proof-4 -->
<!-- corollary-3: body_md -->
Let $H_r$ be diagonal in a graph basis and suppose its eigenvalue on $\lvert G\rangle$
factors through $(|V(G)|,\mathsf P_r(G))$.  Then $H_r$ cannot have zero energy
on every connected graph and positive energy on every disconnected graph.
<!-- end corollary-3 -->
<!-- nogotheorem-4: body_md -->
\label{thm:unitary-attractor}
Let $\{U_s\}_{s\ge0}$ be any family of unitaries on a finite-dimensional
Hilbert space.  For every pair of states $\rho,\sigma$ and every unitarily
invariant norm,
\begin{equation}
 \lVert\!\lVert U_s\rho U_s^\dagger-U_s\sigma U_s^\dagger
 \rVert\!\rVert
 =\lVert\!\lVert\rho-\sigma\rVert\!\rVert.
 \label{eq:isometry}
\end{equation}
Hence two distinct initial states cannot converge under the same unitary
conjugation to one common norm limit.  In particular, no nonempty open set has
a point attractor in trace norm.
<!-- end nogotheorem-4 -->
<!-- proof-5: body_md -->
Equation \eqref{eq:isometry} is unitary invariance.  If both evolved states
converged to the same $\rho_*$, the triangle inequality would force their
constant positive distance to converge to zero.
<!-- end proof-5 -->
<!-- corollary-4: body_md -->
If $P$ is a projection satisfying $[P,U_s]=0$ for all $s$, then
$\operatorname{Tr}[(\mathbf 1-P)U_s\rho U_s^\dagger]=\operatorname{Tr}[(\mathbf 1-P)\rho]$.  Nonzero weight outside
$\operatorname{Ran} P$ cannot disappear.
<!-- end corollary-4 -->
<!-- lemma-1: body_md -->
\label{lem:update-algebra}
For all $e,f\in\mathcal E_N$,
\begin{equation}
 W_e=W_e^\dagger,
 \qquad W_e^2=\mathbf 1,
 \qquad [W_e,W_f]=0.
 \label{eq:update-algebra}
\end{equation}
Consequently
\begin{equation}
 W_N:=\prod_{e\in\mathcal E_N}W_e
 \label{eq:global-update}
\end{equation}
is an order-independent Hermitian involution.
<!-- end lemma-1 -->
<!-- proof-6: body_md -->
All $Q_e$ are diagonal in the common computational basis of the controls.
The relation flips act on distinct pair registers.  The two summands in
\eqref{eq:local-update} have orthogonal control support, so $W_e^2=\mathbf 1$ and
$W_e=W_e^\dagger$.  Common control diagonality and disjoint relation support
give pairwise commutation.
<!-- end proof-6 -->
<!-- construction-1: body_md -->
\label{con:cyclic}
For one scale $E_*>0$, define
\begin{equation}
 \boxed{H^{\mathrm{cyc}}_{N,L}=E_*\left[
 \sum_{t\in\mathbb Z_L}P_t+\lvert 0\rangle\!\langle 0\rvert_{\mathcal T_L}\otimes K_N
 \right].}
 \label{eq:Hcyc}
\end{equation}
<!-- end construction-1 -->
<!-- theorem-1: body_md -->
\label{thm:gauge-ground}
The cyclic Hamiltonian obeys
\begin{equation}
 G_{N,L}^\daggerH^{\mathrm{cyc}}_{N,L} G_{N,L}
 =E_*\left[L_L\otimes\mathbf 1+\lvert 0\rangle\!\langle 0\rvert\otimes K_N\right].
 \label{eq:gauge-reduction}
\end{equation}
It has the unique normalized zero-energy state
\begin{equation}
 \lvert \Psi_{N,L}\rangle=\frac1{\sqrt L}
 \sum_{t=0}^{L-1}\lvert t\rangle\otimes W_N^t\lvert \Omega_N\rangle.
 \label{eq:cyclic-ground}
\end{equation}
<!-- end theorem-1 -->
<!-- proof-7: body_md -->
On the $t$th clock fiber, $G_{N,L}$ multiplies the data vector by $W_N^t$.
The update across $t\to t+1$ cancels because
$W_N^{t+1}=W_NW_N^t$, turning every twisted difference into the ordinary
cycle difference.  The pin lies at $t=0$ and is unchanged, giving
\eqref{eq:gauge-reduction}.

A zero-energy vector is constant in clock after the gauge transformation and
its data vector lies in $\operatorname{ker} K_N=\mathbb C\Omega_N$.  Undoing the gauge gives
\eqref{eq:cyclic-ground}.  Therefore the kernel is one dimensional.
<!-- end proof-7 -->
<!-- theorem-2: body_md -->
\label{thm:complete-spectrum}
The spectrum of the cyclic Hamiltonian, including multiplicity, is
\begin{equation}
 \operatorname{spec}(H^{\mathrm{cyc}}_{N,L}/E_*)=
 \biguplus_{m=0}^{R}\binom Rm\,\operatorname{spec}(A_{L,m}).
 \label{eq:full-spectrum}
\end{equation}
Let
\begin{equation}
 \lambda_k=1-\cos\frac{2\pi k}{L},
 \qquad k=0,\ldots,L-1.
 \label{eq:lambda-k}
\end{equation}
For $z\notin\{\lambda_k\}$, the characteristic polynomial of $A_{L,m}$ is
\begin{equation}
 \det(A_{L,m}-z\mathbf 1)=
 \prod_{k=0}^{L-1}(\lambda_k-z)
 \left[1+\frac mL\sum_{k=0}^{L-1}\frac1{\lambda_k-z}\right],
 \label{eq:secular}
\end{equation}
with the right side understood by polynomial continuation at the apparent
poles.  Equation \eqref{eq:secular} determines every eigenvalue of every data
sector.
<!-- end theorem-2 -->
<!-- proof-8: body_md -->
Diagonalize $K_N$ in its product eigenbasis and use
\eqref{eq:gauge-reduction}; each data eigenvector of weight $m$ carries the
clock operator $A_{L,m}$, with multiplicity $\binom Rm$.  The Fourier basis
diagonalizes $L_L$ with eigenvalues \eqref{eq:lambda-k}, and
$|\langle0|k\rangle|^2=1/L$.  The matrix determinant lemma gives
\eqref{eq:secular}.
<!-- end proof-8 -->
<!-- theorem-3: body_md -->
\label{thm:exact-gap}
Let $L\ge4$ be even.  There is a unique
$\theta_L\in(0,\pi/L)$ satisfying
\begin{equation}
 \tan\frac{L\theta_L}{2}=\frac1{\sin\theta_L}.
 \label{eq:theta-equation}
\end{equation}
The first positive eigenvalue of \eqref{eq:Hcyc} is exactly
\begin{equation}
 \boxed{\Delta_{N,L}=E_*\bigl(1-\cos\theta_L\bigr),}
 \label{eq:exact-gap}
\end{equation}
for every $N\ge2$.  It obeys the sharp elementary bracket
\begin{equation}
 E_*\left(1-\cos\frac\pi{L+2}\right)
 <\Delta_{N,L}<
 E_*\left(1-\cos\frac\pi L\right)
 \label{eq:gap-bracket}
\end{equation}
and the expansion
\begin{equation}
 \Delta_{N,L}=E_*\left[
 \frac{\pi^2}{2L^2}-\frac{2\pi^2}{L^3}+O(L^{-4})
 \right].
 \label{eq:gap-asymptotic}
\end{equation}
<!-- end theorem-3 -->
<!-- proof-9: body_md -->
The $m=0$ block has the constant zero mode and first excitation
$1-\cos(2\pi/L)$.  For $m\ge1$, the lowest eigenvalue of $A_{L,m}$ is
monotone nondecreasing in $m$ by the min--max principle.  It is therefore
enough to solve the ground eigenvalue of $A_{L,1}$.

Write $\mu=1-\cos\theta$ with $0<\theta<\pi/L$ and choose the positive,
reflection-symmetric vector
\begin{equation}
 f_t=\cos\left[\left(\frac L2-t\right)\theta\right],
 \qquad t\in\mathbb Z_L.
 \label{eq:defect-vector}
\end{equation}
Away from $t=0$, the cycle recurrence gives
$L_Lf=(1-\cos\theta)f$.  At the defect site, the eigenvalue equation is
\begin{equation}
 (1+\cos\theta)f_0-f_1=0.
\end{equation}
Substitution of \eqref{eq:defect-vector} reduces this condition to
\eqref{eq:theta-equation}.  On $(0,\pi/L)$ the left side of
\eqref{eq:theta-equation} increases from zero to infinity, while
$1/\sin\theta$ decreases, so the root is unique.  The vector is strictly
positive; irreducibility of the defect Laplacian identifies it as the ground
state of $A_{L,1}$.

At $\theta_0=\pi/(L+2)$,
$\tan(L\theta_0/2)=\cot\theta_0<1/\sin\theta_0$, while the tangent diverges as
$\theta\uparrow\pi/L$.  Thus
$\pi/(L+2)<\theta_L<\pi/L$, proving \eqref{eq:gap-bracket}.  This defect
eigenvalue lies below $1-\cos(\pi/L)$ and hence below the first positive
$m=0$ eigenvalue.  It is therefore the global gap.

Finally, set $\delta_L=\pi-L\theta_L$.  Equation
\eqref{eq:theta-equation} becomes
$\cot(\delta_L/2)=1/\sin[(\pi-\delta_L)/L]$.  Taylor expansion gives
$\delta_L=2\pi/L+O(L^{-2})$, hence
$\theta_L=\pi/L-2\pi/L^2+O(L^{-3})$.  Expanding $1-\cos\theta_L$ yields
\eqref{eq:gap-asymptotic}.
<!-- end proof-9 -->
<!-- theorem-4: body_md -->
\label{thm:certification}
For any state $\rho$,
\begin{align}
 1-\operatorname{Tr}(P_{N,L}\rho)
 &\le\frac{\operatorname{Tr}(\rhoH^{\mathrm{cyc}}_{N,L})}{\Delta_{N,L}},
 \label{eq:energy-fidelity}\\
 \frac12\left\lVert \rho-P_{N,L}\right\rVert_1
 &\le\sqrt{\frac{\operatorname{Tr}(\rhoH^{\mathrm{cyc}}_{N,L})}{\Delta_{N,L}}}.
 \label{eq:trace-cert}
\end{align}
For the Gibbs state
$\rho_\beta=e^{-\betaH^{\mathrm{cyc}}_{N,L}}/\operatorname{Tr}(e^{-\betaH^{\mathrm{cyc}}_{N,L}})$,
\begin{equation}
 1-\operatorname{Tr}(P_{N,L}\rho_\beta)
 \le(D_{N,L}-1)e^{-\beta\Delta_{N,L}}.
 \label{eq:gibbs-cert}
\end{equation}
<!-- end theorem-4 -->
<!-- proof-10: body_md -->
The spectral theorem gives
$H^{\mathrm{cyc}}_{N,L}\ge\Delta_{N,L}(\mathbf 1-P_{N,L})$, proving
\eqref{eq:energy-fidelity}.  The trace-distance bound follows from the
Fuchs--van de Graaf inequality for a pure reference state
\cite{NielsenChuang2010}.  For the Gibbs state, every excited Boltzmann weight
is at most $e^{-\beta\Delta_{N,L}}$, and there are at most
$D_{N,L}-1$ excited levels counting multiplicity.
<!-- end proof-10 -->
<!-- theorem-5: body_md -->
\label{thm:stability}
Let $V=V^\dagger$ and
$\widetilde H=H^{\mathrm{cyc}}_{N,L}+V$.  If
$\varepsilon:=\left\lVert V\right\rVert<\Delta_{N,L}/2$, then the ground eigenvalue of
$\widetilde H$ is simple, its gap satisfies
\begin{equation}
 \widetilde\Delta\ge\Delta_{N,L}-2\varepsilon,
 \label{eq:perturbed-gap}
\end{equation}
and its rank-one ground projector $\widetilde P$ obeys
\begin{equation}
 \left\lVert \widetilde P-P_{N,L}\right\rVert
 \le\min\left\{1,\frac{\varepsilon}{\Delta_{N,L}-2\varepsilon}\right\}.
 \label{eq:projector-bound}
\end{equation}
In particular, the admissible full-operator-norm window scales as $L^{-2}$.
<!-- end theorem-5 -->
<!-- proof-11: body_md -->
Weyl inequalities shift each ordered eigenvalue by at most $\varepsilon$,
which gives \eqref{eq:perturbed-gap} and simplicity.  For the projector bound, write $P=P_{N,L}$, $Q=\mathbf 1-P$, and let
$\lvert \varphi\rangle$ be a normalized perturbed ground state of energy
$\widetilde E_0$.  Weyl's bound gives
$|\widetilde E_0|\le\varepsilon$.
The compression
$Q(\widetilde H-\widetilde E_0)Q$ is bounded below by
$(\Delta_{N,L}-2\varepsilon)Q$ on $\operatorname{Ran} Q$.  Projecting the
eigenvalue equation onto $\operatorname{Ran} Q$ therefore gives
$\left\lVert Q\varphi\right\rVert\le\varepsilon/(\Delta_{N,L}-2\varepsilon)$.
For rank-one orthogonal projectors
$\left\lVert \widetilde P-P\right\rVert=\left\lVert Q\varphi\right\rVert\le1$, yielding
\eqref{eq:projector-bound}; cf. standard matrix perturbation theory
\cite{Bhatia1997}.
<!-- end proof-11 -->
<!-- construction-2: body_md -->
\label{con:boolean}
Define
\begin{equation}
 \boxed{H^{\mathrm{B}}_N=E_*\sum_{e\in\mathcal E_N}h_e.}
 \label{eq:Hboolean}
\end{equation}
Every $h_e$ acts on one clock qubit, one relation qubit, and the two endpoint
controls.  Thus the interaction arity is at most four, independent of $N$.
No order on the pair set appears.
<!-- end construction-2 -->
<!-- theorem-6: body_md -->
\label{thm:boolean-solution}
The terms $h_e$ commute for distinct pairs.  The complete ground space of
\eqref{eq:Hboolean} has orthonormal basis
\begin{equation}
 \lvert \Phi_c\rangle=\lvert c\rangle_{\mathcal C}\otimes
 \bigotimes_{e\in\mathcal E_N}\lvert \phi_{q_e(c)}\rangle_{\mathcal T_e\mathcal R_e},
 \qquad c\in\{0,1\}^N,
 \label{eq:boolean-ground}
\end{equation}
so $\dim\operatorname{ker}H^{\mathrm{B}}_N=2^N$.  Its full spectrum is the additive multiset generated
by
\begin{equation}
 \left\{0,\ 1-\frac1{\sqrt2},\ 1,\ 1+\frac1{\sqrt2}\right\}E_*
 \label{eq:local-spectrum}
\end{equation}
for each of the $M$ pairs, repeated over the $2^N$ control blocks.  In
particular,
\begin{equation}
 \boxed{\Delta_N^{\mathrm B}=E_*\left(1-\frac1{\sqrt2}\right)}
 \label{eq:boolean-gap}
\end{equation}
for every $N\ge2$.
<!-- end theorem-6 -->
<!-- proof-12: body_md -->
The control projectors $Q_e$ are simultaneously diagonal.  Distinct terms
$h_e$ and $h_f$ act on disjoint clock--relation pairs, so they commute even
when their endpoint sets overlap.

Fix a control string $c$.  The local term is either
\begin{align}
 h_0&=\frac12(\mathbf 1-X\otimes\mathbf 1)+\lvert 0\rangle\!\langle 0\rvert\otimes\lvert 1\rangle\!\langle 1\rvert,
 \label{eq:h0}\\
 h_1&=\frac12(\mathbf 1-X\otimes X)+\lvert 0\rangle\!\langle 0\rvert\otimes\lvert 1\rangle\!\langle 1\rvert.
 \label{eq:h1}
\end{align}
A CNOT from the clock qubit to the relation qubit conjugates $h_0$ to $h_1$.
In the relation-$0$ block, $h_0$ has eigenvalues $0,1$; in the relation-$1$
block it has matrix
\begin{equation}
 \begin{pmatrix}3/2&-1/2\\-1/2&1/2\end{pmatrix}
\end{equation}
with eigenvalues $1\pm1/\sqrt2$.  The unique local ground vectors are exactly
\eqref{eq:local-ground-vectors}.  Tensoring the unique local ground vector for
each pair yields \eqref{eq:boolean-ground}, and no additional zero modes are
possible.  Additivity of commuting pair blocks gives the full spectrum and
\eqref{eq:boolean-gap}.
<!-- end proof-12 -->
<!-- corollary-5: body_md -->
\label{cor:q-sector}
The ground space of $H_{N,q}^{\mathrm B}$ is
\begin{equation}
 \operatorname{span}\{\Phi_c:|c|=q\},
 \qquad
 \dim\operatorname{ker} H_{N,q}^{\mathrm B}=\binom Nq,
 \label{eq:q-ground}
\end{equation}
and its gap remains $E_*(1-2^{-1/2})$.  The normalized vector
\begin{equation}
 \lvert \Phi_{N,q}^{\mathrm{sym}}\rangle=\binom Nq^{-1/2}
 \sum_{|c|=q}\lvert \Phi_c\rangle
 \label{eq:symmetric-history}
\end{equation}
spans the one-dimensional $S_N$-invariant subspace of this orbit sector.  For $q=0$ or
$q=N$, the ground state is unique.
<!-- end corollary-5 -->
<!-- proof-13: body_md -->
The operator $C_q$ commutes with $H^{\mathrm{B}}_N$, vanishes exactly on control strings
of weight $q$, and has first positive eigenvalue one.  Since the Boolean gap is
smaller than one, adding $C_q$ does not change the gap.  Transitivity of $S_N$
on the weight-$q$ strings makes the invariant subspace one-dimensional.
<!-- end proof-13 -->
<!-- proposition-1: body_md -->
\label{prop:clock-memory}
Suppose a sharp order-free clock assigns mutually orthogonal clock events to
all subsets $S\subseteq\mathcal E_N$ of $M$ independently recordable commuting updates.
Then
\begin{equation}
 \dim\mathcal T\ge2^M,
 \qquad
 \log_2\dim\mathcal T\ge M.
 \label{eq:clock-lower-bound}
\end{equation}
The Boolean clock \eqref{eq:boolean-clock} saturates both bounds.
<!-- end proposition-1 -->
<!-- proof-14: body_md -->
There are $2^M$ subsets, and a Hilbert space containing $2^M$ mutually
orthogonal nonzero vectors has dimension at least $2^M$.  The tensor product of
$M$ clock qubits has exactly that dimension.
<!-- end proof-14 -->
<!-- theorem-7: body_md -->
\label{thm:permutation}
For every $\pi\in S_N$,
\begin{align}
 [U_\pi,H^{\mathrm{cyc}}_{N,L}]&=0, &
 [U_\pi,H^{\mathrm{B}}_N]&=0,\label{eq:permutation}\\
 U_\pi\lvert \Psi_{N,L}\rangle&=\lvert \Psi_{N,L}\rangle.&&
\end{align}
Moreover $U_\pi\lvert \Phi_c\rangle=\lvert \Phi_{\pi c}\rangle$ and
$U_\pi\lvert \Phi_{N,q}^{\mathrm{sym}}\rangle=\lvert \Phi_{N,q}^{\mathrm{sym}}\rangle$.
<!-- end theorem-7 -->
<!-- proof-15: body_md -->
Conjugation permutes the family $\{Q_e,W_e\}_{e\in\mathcal E_N}$ and the corresponding
clock--relation factors.  Every Hamiltonian is a sum or product over the full
pair orbit.  The initial cyclic state is symmetric within each register type,
and the Boolean ground vectors transform by relabeling the control string.
<!-- end proof-15 -->
<!-- theorem-8: body_md -->
\label{thm:state-concentration}
For every density operator \(\rho\) and every labeled graph basis vector
\(\lvert G\rangle\),
\begin{equation}
 \boxed{
 \langle G\rvert\rho\lvert G\rangle
 \le \frac1{M_G}+\delta_{\rm st}(\rho).}
 \label{eq:state-concentration}
\end{equation}
Consequently, concentration
\(\langle G\rvert\rho\lvert G\rangle\ge1-\varepsilon\) requires
\begin{equation}
 \delta_{\rm st}(\rho)
 \ge1-\varepsilon-\frac1{M_G}.
 \label{eq:state-asymmetry-cost}
\end{equation}
<!-- end theorem-8 -->
<!-- proof-16: body_md -->
Convexity of trace distance gives
\[
 \frac12\left\lVert \rho-\mathcal G(\rho)\right\rVert_1
 \le\frac1{N!}\sum_{\pi}\frac12
 \left\lVert \rho-U_\pi\rho U_\pi^\dagger\right\rVert_1
 \le\delta_{\rm st}(\rho).
\]
Because the twirled state is constant on the orbit diagonal,
\[
 \langle G\rvert\mathcal G(\rho)\lvert G\rangle
 =\frac1{M_G}\sum_{H\in\mathcal O_G}\langle H\rvert\rho\lvert H\rangle
 \le\frac1{M_G}.
\]
The variational characterization of trace distance bounds the change of the
projector probability \(\lvert G\rangle\!\langle G\rvert\), proving
\eqref{eq:state-concentration}; rearrangement gives
\eqref{eq:state-asymmetry-cost}.
<!-- end proof-16 -->
<!-- corollary-6: body_md -->
\label{cor:relative-labeling-cost}
Suppose $M_G>1$ and let
\(p=\langle G\rvert\rho\lvert G\rangle\ge M_G^{-1}\).  Then
\begin{equation}
 A_{\rm rel}(\rho)
 \ge
 p\log(pM_G)+(1-p)\log\!\left(
 \frac{1-p}{1-M_G^{-1}}
 \right).
 \label{eq:relative-labeling-cost}
\end{equation}
For the pure labeled state \(\rho=\lvert G\rangle\!\langle G\rvert\) with $M_G>1$, equality gives
\begin{equation}
 A_{\rm rel}(\lvert G\rangle\!\langle G\rvert)=\log M_G.
\end{equation}
<!-- end corollary-6 -->
<!-- proof-17: body_md -->
Apply data processing for relative entropy to the binary measurement
\(\{\lvert G\rangle\!\langle G\rvert,\mathbf 1-\lvert G\rangle\!\langle G\rvert\}\).  Its second-state success probability is
at most \(M_G^{-1}\).  For fixed \(p\ge M_G^{-1}\), binary relative entropy
is decreasing in the reference probability on \((0,p]\), which gives
\eqref{eq:relative-labeling-cost}.  For \(\lvert G\rangle\!\langle G\rvert\), the twirl is the
uniform mixture on \(\mathcal O_G\), and the stated equality is immediate.
<!-- end proof-17 -->
